description: Test coverage, isolation, naming, and hygiene standards. Applied by the coder agent when writing tests and checked by the pr-reviewer agent against every diff that introduces or modifies tested code.

standards.title: New public behaviour requires at least one test
standards.description: Every new public function, method, class, or API endpoint introduced in a diff must have at least one corresponding test that exercises the primary success path. Untested public behaviour is not shippable.
standards.rationale: Code without tests cannot be refactored safely, cannot be verified by CI, and will silently break as the codebase evolves. The cost of writing a test at authoring time is a fraction of the cost of debugging a regression later.
acceptance_criteria: For every new public function or method in the diff, at least one test in the same diff (or an existing test file) exercises its primary happy-path behaviour.
For every new HTTP route, CLI command, or public API endpoint, at least one test asserts the expected response for a valid request.
Tests for new behaviour are added in the same PR as the behaviour — not deferred to a follow-up.
Private functions and internal helpers that are only reachable via tested public interfaces are exempt from direct test requirements.
anti_patterns: Introducing a new function and leaving the test file unchanged.
Adding a new API endpoint with only a placeholder '# TODO: add tests' comment.
Implementing a new feature and planning to 'add tests in the next PR'.
Marking a function as private solely to avoid the test requirement when it has externally observable effects.

standards.title: Unit tests must not make real network or filesystem calls
standards.description: Tests in the unit-test layer must not perform real HTTP requests, DNS lookups, database queries, or filesystem writes outside a designated temp directory. All I/O must be replaced by mocks, fakes, or fixtures injected at test setup.
standards.rationale: Tests that rely on real external state are non-deterministic, slow, and fail in CI environments without network access. They also create hidden dependencies between tests and external systems that are hard to reproduce on failure.
acceptance_criteria: No test in the unit-test layer makes an outbound HTTP request (requests.get, urllib, httpx, fetch) without mocking the transport layer.
No test reads from or writes to paths outside of tempfile.mkdtemp(), pytest's tmp_path, or an equivalent isolated temporary directory.
No test opens a real database connection — database calls are replaced by in-memory databases (sqlite :memory:), fakes, or mock objects.
Network or filesystem mocking is applied at the lowest practical boundary (e.g. patching the HTTP adapter, not the entire requests module).
Integration tests that intentionally exercise real I/O are placed in a separate directory (tests/integration/) and excluded from the default pytest run.
anti_patterns: A unit test that calls requests.get('https://api.example.com/...') without patching.
A test that writes to a hardcoded path like /tmp/test_output.json that could collide across parallel test runs.
Mocking an entire external library (mock.patch('requests')) instead of patching at the HTTP adapter boundary.
A test that passes only when a specific database server is reachable, with no skip or xfail guard.

standards.title: Each test asserts exactly one behaviour
standards.description: Each test function must assert a single, named behaviour. Tests must not be assertion-free, and must not bundle multiple unrelated scenarios into one test body.
standards.rationale: Tests that verify multiple behaviours produce ambiguous failure messages — a reader cannot tell which behaviour broke. Assertion-free tests always pass, giving false confidence. One behaviour per test makes failures self-documenting.
acceptance_criteria: Every test function in the diff contains at least one explicit assertion (assert, pytest.raises, unittest assertion method).

Each test function asserts a single logical behaviour — multiple assertions are permitted only when they collectively verify one indivisible outcome (e.g. asserting both status code and response body for one request).
Test functions that verify multiple distinct scenarios (happy path AND error path) are split into separate test functions.
No test uses a bare pass or returns early without asserting anything.
anti_patterns: A test named test_user_flow that exercises login, update, and logout in sequence with assertions scattered throughout.
A test function with zero assert statements (assertion-free test).
A parametrized test where some parameter combinations test happy paths and others test error paths in the same assertion block.
Using a loop to run multiple independent scenarios inside a single test function.

standards.title: Test names encode scenario and expected outcome
standards.description: Test function names must describe the condition under test and the expected outcome in a form that reads as a specification. Names must not be generic (test_1, test_it, test_works) or repeat only the function name being tested.
standards.rationale: A test name is the first and often only information a developer sees when a test fails in CI. A descriptive name eliminates the need to read the test body to understand what broke and what the expected behaviour was.
acceptance_criteria: Every test function name in the diff follows the pattern test_<scenario>_<expected_outcome> or a domain-appropriate equivalent that encodes both the condition and the result.
No test function is named test_<function_name> with no further qualification (e.g. test_parse, test_send).
No test function is named with a numeric suffix (test_1, test_case_2) as the only differentiator.
Class-based test suites name the class after the unit under test (TestClassName) and name methods after the behaviour (test_raises_when_input_is_empty).
anti_patterns: def test_1(), def test_2() for two related cases.
def test_parse() with no description of what input or what outcome is expected.
def test_it_works() — too vague to diagnose on failure.
def test_user() when the test actually verifies that creating a user with a duplicate email raises ValueError.
